8    KINDRED BRAVELY,                                                         
                                     ORDER DENYING PLAINTIFF’S EX             
9                  Plaintiff,        PARTE MOTION FOR ALTERNATIVE             
                                     SERVICE WITHOUT PREJUDICE                
10         v.                                                                  
11    SHENZHEN CONGLIN E-                                                      
     COMMERCE CO., LTD (dba                                                   
12    SMARTLIN) and SHENZHEN LUTE                                              
     INNOVATIONS TECHNOLOGY CO.,                                              
13    LTD. fka SHENZHEN                                                        
     LUTEJIACHENG NETWORK                                                     
14    TECHNOLOGY CO., LTD., aka                                                
     SHENZHEN LUTEJIACHENG                                                    
15    TECHNOLOGY, CO., LTD. aka                                                
     SHENZHEN ROOT TECHNOLOGY                                                 
16    CO. LTD. aka SHENZHEN ROOT E-                                            
     COMMERCE CO., LTD. (collectively                                         
17    dba MOMCOZY),                                                            
18                   Defendants.                                               
19                                                                             
         This matter comes before the Court on Plaintiff Akerson Enterprises LLC’s 
20                                                                             
    motion for alternative service on Defendants. Dkt. No. 3. For the reasons explained 
21                                                                             
    below, Kindred’s motion is DENIED.                                        
22                                                                             
23                                                                             
1                          1.  BACKGROUND                                     
2        Akerson Enterprises LLC d/b/a Kindred Bravely (“Kindred”) is a women’s 

3   apparel company that specializes in “comfortable and stylish clothing” for pregnant 
4   and nursing mothers. Dkt. 1 ¶ 11. Kindred holds a patent for a “multi-layer nursing 
5   bra.” Id. ¶¶ 18-20. Kindred alleges Defendants—who “market themselves     
6   collectively as ‘Momcozy’”—infringe on its patent by importing and selling the 
7   product “Upgrade 4-in-1 Pumping Bra” with a “CozyFitClasp.” Id. ¶¶ 26–27.  
8   Kindred also alleges Defendants “deceptively manipulat[e] the Amazon.com ASIN 

9   system.” Id. at 3.                                                        
10        Kindred identifies Defendants as Chinese entities, represented by U.S. 
11   counsel, with pro hac vice Chinese counsel in another case pending in this District: 
12   Shenzhen Root Tech. Co. et al. v. Chiaro Tech., Ltd., (W.D. Wash. Case No. 2:23-cv-
13   631-KKE). Id. at 4. Kindred attached pleadings and notes from Chiaro in support of 
14   this motion, purporting to show that Defendants’ counsel “have provided email 
15   addresses for purposes of service in Chiaro.” Id.                         

16        Kindred also provides a screenshot of the webpage https://momcozy.com/
17   pages/contact-us. Dkt. No. 4-4 at 3. The screenshot includes the email address 
18   “support@momcozy.com.” Dkt. No. 4-4 at 4. At the bottom of the webpage, there is a 
19   reference to a “Colorado Office” and a “Root Technology Ltd.,” with a Colorado 
20   mailing address. Id. Kindred includes a screenshot from Colorado’s Secretary of 
21   State that lists “Root technology ltd.,” which is the same Colorado mailing address 

22   listed on the momcozy.com webpage. Dkt. No. 4-7 at 2. The screenshot also shows 
23   the name of a registered agent, Liqiang Zeng. Id. Despite this, Kindred explains 
1   that “it is Defendant Shenzhen Lute that provides the privacy notice on the 
2   Momcozy website, not the Colorado entity . . ., and it is the Defendants that import, 

3   offer for sale, and sell Momcozy’s products in the United States.” Dkt. No. 3 at 3. 
4        Kindred requests permission to serve Defendants by email, and it states that 
5   it will “shortly file a motion for preliminary injunction to stop [Defendants’] patent 
6   infringement and . . . unfair competition.” Id.                           
7                             2.  ANALYSIS                                    
8   2.1  Legal standards.                                                     
         Rule 4(f) permits service on individuals in foreign countries by (1) any 
9                                                                             
    internationally agreed means of service, such as the Hague Convention; (2) if there 
10                                                                             
    is no internationally agreed means, by a method that comports with the foreign 
11                                                                             
    country’s law; or (3) by “other means not prohibited by international agreement, as 
12                                                                             
    the court orders.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(f).                                  
13                                                                             
         Kindred argues that it should be allowed to serve Defendants via email 
14                                                                             
    because “[s]ervice via the Hague Convention would take much too long and preclude 
15                                                                             
    Plaintiff from obtaining meaningful injunctive relief.” Dkt. No. 3 at 4. The Court 
16                                                                             
    construes Kindred’s request as seeking permission to serve Defendants under 
17                                                                             
    Rule 4(f)(3). There’s nothing that stops Kindred from petitioning the court for email 
18                                                                             
    service before attempting other means of service—indeed, “service of process under 
19                                                                             
    Rule 4(f)(3) is neither a ‘last resort nor ‘extraordinary relief.’” Rio Props., Inc. v. Rio 
20                                                                             
    Int’l Interlink, 284 F.3d 1007, 1015 (9th Cir. 2002). But Rule 4(f)(3) only authorizes 
21                                                                             
    service by “means not prohibited by international agreement” and thus cannot be 
22                                                                             
    used as an end run around the Hague Convention and its restrictions. Rio Props., 
23                                                                             
1   Inc., 284 F.3d at 1015 n.4 (“A federal court would be prohibited from issuing a Rule 
2   4(f)(3) order in contravention of an international agreement, including the Hague 

3   Convention referenced in Rule 4(f)(1).”); see Volkswagenwerk Aktiengesellschaft v. 
4   Schlunk, 486 U.S. 694, 699 (1988) (“[C]ompliance with the Convention is mandatory 
5   in all cases to which it applies.”).                                      
6        As the party requesting alternative service under Rule 4(f)(3), Kindred must 
7   show that “the facts and circumstances of the present case necessitated the district 
8   court’s intervention.” Rio Props., Inc., 284 F.3d at 1016. Kindred must also show 

9   that the requested method of service “comport[s] with constitutional notions of due 
10   process.” Id.                                                             
11        Kindred cites a few cases in support of its request but assumes without much 
12   analysis that service may be had on a Chinese defendant via email. The Court does 
13   not share this assumption and begins its analysis with the Hague Convention, as 
14   the Convention is the starting point in “all cases, in civil or commercial matters, 
15   where there is occasion to transmit a judicial or extrajudicial document for service 

16   abroad.” Water Splash, Inc. v. Menon, 581 U.S. 271, 276 (2017).           
17                                                                             
    2.2  The Hague Convention.                                                
18                                                                             
         Rule 4(f)(1) states that service may be had on any individual or business by 
19                                                                             
    the Hague Convention. China is a member of the Hague Convention. See      
20                                                                             
    Contracting Parties, Hague Conference on Private International Law,       
21                                                                             
    https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=17 (last visited 
22                                                                             
    June 13, 2024). “[T]he Hague Service Convention specifies certain approved 
23                                                                             
1   methods of service and ‘pre-empts inconsistent methods of service’ wherever it 
2   applies.” Water Splash, 581 U.S. at 273 (quoting Schlunk, 486 U.S. at 699).  

3        Article 10(a) authorizes service of judicial documents by “postal channels” so 
4   long as the “State of destination does not object.” Hague Convention, art. 10(a). But 
5   neither the Convention nor Article 10(a) “speak in specific terms of service by e-
6   mail, fax, or other means of delivery unknown in the 1960’s.” Luxottica Grp. S.p.A. 
7   v. Partnerships & Unincorporated Ass’ns Identified on Schedule “A”, 391 F. Supp. 3d 
8   816, 825 (N.D. Ill. 2019). China, “[l]ike many signatories to the Hague Convention,” 

9   Nexon Korea Corp. v. Ironmace Co., No. C23-576-MLP, 2023 WL 3599548, at *2 
10   (W.D. Wash. May 23, 2023), objects to Article 10(a) and service through postal 
11   channels. Smart Study Co. v. Acuteye-Us, 620 F. Supp. 3d 1382, 1394 (S.D.N.Y. 
12   2022), appeal dismissed sub nom. Smart Study Co. v. HAPPY PARTY-001, No. 22-
13   1810-CV, 2023 WL 3220461 (2d Cir. May 3, 2023) (“China has objected to service by 
14   postal channels.”); see HCCH, Status Table 14 Convention of 15 November 1965 on 
15   the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial 

16   Matters, https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=17 
17   (last visited, July 12, 2024).                                            
18        “Courts have split on whether such an objection also prohibits service by e-
19   mail, which is not explicitly listed in Article 10(a).” Anova Applied Elecs., Inc. v. 
20   Hong King Grp., Ltd., 334 F.R.D. 465, 470 (D. Mass. 2020). One camp holds that 
21   because “the Hague Convention outlines specific methods of service,” any “methods 

22   of service that are not specifically authorized are impermissible under the 
23   Convention.” Smart Study Co., 620 F. Supp. 3d at 1393. These courts reason that 
1   “[t]he Convention … doesn’t simply offer options for service abroad—options that 
2   plaintiffs can resort to or not at their discretion. Rather, unless an exception 

3   applies, the Convention-delineated methods of service … are exclusive.” Facebook, 
4   Inc. v. 9 Xiu Network (Shenzhen) Tech. Co., 480 F. Supp. 3d 977, 983 (N.D. Cal. 
5   2020).                                                                    
6        Other courts reject this notion. For example, the Tenth Circuit held in 
7   Compania de Inversiones Mercantiles, S.A. v. Grupo Cementos de Chihuahua S.A.B. 
8   de C.V., 970 F.3d 1269, 1294 (10th Cir. 2020), that “the relevant inquiry under Rule 

9   4(f)(3) is not whether the [international] agreement affirmatively endorses service,” 
10   but “whether the alternative service method in question is ‘prohibited’ by the 
11   agreement.” Although the court did not address email service in particular, it found 
12   that if “the Convention does not contain a specific prohibition on [a] form of service,” 
13   a district court could properly authorize that form of service under Rule 4(f)(3). Id. 
14   at 1294–95. Regarding email service on a Chinese defendant specifically, the Fifth 
15   Circuit has found that it does not violate the Hague Convention and can be 

16   appropriate under Rule 4(f)(3). Nagravision SA v. Gotech Int’l Tech. Ltd., 882 F.3d 
17   494, 498 (5th Cir. 2018).                                                 
18        This is the better approach and the prevailing view among the courts in this 
19   district that have addressed the subject. See, e.g., Amazon.com Inc. v. Bamb Awns, 
20   No. C22-402-MLP, 2023 WL 2837076, at *2 (W.D. Wash. Apr. 7, 2023) (“Whether or 
21   not the Hague Convention applies, this Court and others have concluded that email 

22   service on individuals located in China … is not prohibited by [the Hague 
23   Convention] or any other international agreement.”); Rubie’s Costume Co., Inc. v. 
1   Yiwu Hua Hao Toys Co., No. 2:18-CV-01530-RAJ, 2019 WL 6310564, at *2 (W.D. 
2   Wash. Nov. 25, 2019) (“the Court finds that Plaintiff’s proposed methods of 

3   alternative service [i.e., email] are not expressly prohibited by international 
4   agreement.”); but see Amazon.com Inc. v. Robojap Techs. LLC, No. C20-694 MJP, 
5   2021 WL 4893426, at *2 (W.D. Wash. Oct. 20, 2021) (email service on defendant 
6   located in India was improper because India objects to Article 10’s provisions for 
7   service by postal channels).1                                             
8        Given the lack of binding precedent on this issue and the Court’s agreement 

9   with the majority view of courts in this district, the Court finds that email service to 
10   a foreign defendant in China is allowed under Rule 4(f)(3) because the Hague 
11   Convention does not expressly prohibit it.                                
12        And as to Kindred’s request to effect service by emailing Defendants’ U.S.-
13   based counsel, the Hague Convention does not apply in any event. Schlunk, 486 
14                                                                             

15   1 By its plain terms, the Hague Convention does not prohibit email service, with 
    whether the service is prohibited being the primary inquiry under Rule 4(f)(3). Still, 
16   some courts have found that “China’s objection to service via ‘postal channels’ … 
    necessarily encompass[es] an objection to service via email. Smart Study Co., 620 F. 
17   Supp. 3d at 1394. “Reading a prohibition on service ‘by postal channels’ to prohibit 
    service by email,” however, “presents obvious textual difficulty.” Purple Innovation 
18   v. Foshan Dirani Design Furniture, No. 2:22-CV-620-HCN-DAO, 2024 WL 1347356, 
    at *4 (D. Utah Mar. 29, 2024) (citing Anova, 334 F.R.D. at 470). Besides, there are 
19   many sound reasons why a signatory state might object to service by postal mail but 
    not by email. Id. Email is instantaneous, it does not require physical intrusion into 
20   the receiving country’s territory, it may be more reliable than postal mail, it is 
    easily tracked, the recipient can confirm receipt and whether they are in fact the 
21   correct recipient, and—in the case of online retailers overseas—it may be the only 
    practical means of contact. See id. (collecting cases); see also Hangzhou Chic 
22   Intelligent Tech. Co. v. Partnerships & Unincorporated Associations Identified on 
    Schedule A, No. 20 C 4806, 2021 WL 1222783, at *3 (N.D. Ill. Apr. 1, 2021) (“unlike 
23   postal service, email does not require physical intrusion on Chinese territory[.]”). 
1   U.S. at 708 (1988) (“Where service on a domestic agent is valid and complete …, our 
2   inquiry ends and the Convention has no further implications.”); United States v. 

3   Aquatherm GmbH, No. 3:22-CV-1101-JR, 2023 WL 3018936, at *2 (D. Or. Apr. 20, 
4   2023) (“The Hague Convention … is not applicable when service … is done   
5   domestically under Rule 4(f)(3).”).                                       
6        In sum, the Court concludes that service by email is not prohibited by 
7   international agreement. Before authorizing service under Rule 4(f)(3), however, the 
8   Court must still determine whether the facts and circumstances here necessitate 

9   court intervention and whether the proposed method of service comports with due 
10   process. Rio Props., 284 F.3d at 1016.                                    
11                                                                             
    2.3  Kindred fails to demonstrate why Court intervention is required      
         under the present facts and circumstances.                           
12                                                                             
         Even if alternative service is permitted under Rule 4(f)(3), “[t]he party 
13                                                                             
    requesting alternate service must ‘demonstrate that the facts and circumstances of 
14                                                                             
    the present case necessitate the district court’s intervention.’” Amazon.com, Inc. v. 
15                                                                             
    Tian, No. 2:21-CV-00159-TL, 2022 WL 486267, at *2 (W.D. Wash. Feb. 17, 2022) 
16                                                                             
    (citing Rio Props, Inc., 284 F.3d at 1016). Factors that would justify alternative 
17                                                                             
    service include whether the defendant was evading service and whether the 
18                                                                             
    plaintiff had been in contact with the defendant. See Rubie's Costume, 2019 WL 
19                                                                             
    6310564, at *2; see also Tian, 2022 WL 486267, at *3 (citing Rio Props, Inc., 284 
20                                                                             
    F.3d at 1016). Urgency provides another grounds for resorting to a “special method 
21                                                                             
    of service” under Rule 4(f)(3). Rio Props., 284 F.3d at 1015.             
22                                                                             
23                                                                             
1        Kindred has failed to demonstrate that the facts and circumstances of this 
2   case warrant special service right now. To be sure, Kindred argues in conclusory 

3   fashion that its need to serve Defendants with process is urgent, but nowhere does 
4   it explain the basis for the urgency. The Court will not presume. Nor does Kindred 
5   allege or show that Defendants have evaded service. In fact, the record suggests 
6   that Kindred has made no attempts to serve Defendants through the Hague   
7   Convention or otherwise. See Dkt. No. 3; see also Rubie’s Costume, 2019 WL 
8   6310564, at *3 (Denying alternative service to remaining defendants when, “[f]rom 

9   the record, it does not appear that Rubie’s has attempted service on these 
10   defendants at all.”). Similarly, despite Kindred’s knowledge of Defendant’s U.S. 
11   based counsel, it neither alleges nor demonstrates that tried to arrange service 
12   through Defendants’ domestic counsel. See id.                             
13        On this record, it appears that Kindred requests alternative service merely 
14   because it is easier and quicker than other means of service, but “the desire for 
15   expedience and efficiency alone is not sufficient to justify alternative service.” Tian, 

16   2022 WL 486267, at *2. Because Kindred has failed to demonstrate that the 
17   circumstances require alternative service at this time, it need not consider the effect 
18   of Kindred’s request on Defendants’ due process rights.                   
19                           3.  CONCLUSION                                    
20        For the reasons stated above, Kindred’s ex parte motion for alternative 
21   service is DENIED without prejudice. Plaintiffs may refile their motion to try to 

22   demonstrate that their request for alternative service is warranted by the facts and 
23                                                                             
1   circumstances of the case and that its requested means of service comport with due 
2   process.                                                                  

3        Dated this 23 day of July, 2024.                                     
4                                      A                                      
                                       Jamal N. Whitehead                     
5                                      United States District Judge           
6                                                                             
7                                                                             
8
